card.problem: Walk through the project you really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.adopted: none
card.heard: other options, why not, and how I knew it worked after release
card.say: There were two other options. First, I could let the server keep the resume point, so the app sends nothing and the server decides where to continue. Second, I could ask for the whole plan again on every reconnect and replace everything on screen. I didn't pick the server-side point because the backend team was small and it added state to every request. I didn't pick the full reload because users would lose the cards they already had and wait again. I kept the client-side point, but saved it only after the card was drawn, and added the guard for a bad saved point. After release, I checked it with our tests and the logs from real users; they only cover the cases we saw, so they can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.

turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: Android client as Screen, ViewModel, Repository and Local DB; server owns the authoritative ledger
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer history and details in scope; cached reads work offline", "Submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger", "Top up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: request in flight, user switches to account C, A's old response arrives — what goes wrong on Android, how to prevent
card.say: The old response can land on account C's screen. That's the main risk. The ViewModel and the repository are still alive, so a late callback writes A's transfer result into whatever screen is showing now. A second risk is the cache: A's balance and history could be written into the local database while C is signed in. To prevent it, I'd tag every request, cache write and callback with the account and a session generation. A's committed transfer stays on the server, and it comes back from A's own history when A signs in again.
card.then: Next: how the ViewModel and repository get that session generation, if you want to go deeper.

more: The repository also needs to cancel A's in-flight call when the session generation changes.

card.adopted: Android client as Screen, ViewModel, Repository and Local DB; server owns the authoritative ledger
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer history and details in scope; cached reads work offline", "Submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger", "Top up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: model said success before the server answered, then the server rejects it
card.say: The chat message is never the record. The result screen reads only the server's transfer record, so a "succeeded" line from the model is just text. When the server later rejects the transfer, the app shows a clear failure from that record, and the ledger stays at A 100 dollars and B 0. I'd also mark that chat message as not confirmed, so the user sees the correction in the same place. And the model should never say a payment succeeded before the server answers; it should say it's checking. If the model calls the payment tool again, that call maps to the same intent and client ID, so it can never create a second transfer.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The users were travelers on the KKday app.
Candidate: They had a destination, a budget and a number of days, but planning by hand took a lot of time.
Candidate: They had to work out the cost, search products one by one and put the plan together.
Candidate: So the planner gave them a bookable plan in one place.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan: the agent design, the product and order tools, and the core backend.
Candidate: It ended at the Android side of the result display, which I wrote with the app team.
Candidate: I was the technical lead for a five-person project, and I reported to the head of the Tour team.
Interviewer: On the KKday planner, you said your responsibility ended at the Android result display you wrote with the app team — so which exact parts did you build yourself versus the team?
Candidate: I built the agent design, the product and order tools, and the core backend myself.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream of the trip plan.
Candidate: The app team built the screens around it, and we agreed the card format together.
Candidate: The other four people worked on the app screens, testing and the product side.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself is the Android code that reads the SSE stream.
Candidate: A user enters a destination, budget and days, and taps plan.
Candidate: The app opens the stream and reads each event as it arrives.
Candidate: The first day card shows while the rest is still being made.
Candidate: I parse each event off the main thread and push the cards out through StateFlow, so the screen updates one card at a time.
Candidate: The stream can break halfway.
Candidate: Then the app shows the cards it already has, and it keeps the last good state.
Candidate: It reconnects and asks for the rest of the plan.
Candidate: If the retry limit is reached, the user sees a safe fallback instead of a broken screen.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was a plan that broke halfway and then showed a day twice after reconnecting.
Candidate: I first suspected the server was sending the whole plan again.
Candidate: The log showed the app was asking from the wrong point, because it saved the last card before the card was fully drawn.
Candidate: So I moved the save to after the card was shown, and the duplicate days stopped.
Candidate: I'd also add a guard for a bad saved position: if the saved point is missing or corrupt, the app reloads the plan from the start instead of resuming from a bad point.

Interviewer: You said the log showed the app was asking from the wrong point — what in that log actually told you it was the saved position and not the server resending, and how did you confirm the fix held in production rather than just in your repro?
Candidate: The log showed the same day card being requested twice, and the saved position was one card behind.
Candidate: So the server wasn't resending the plan; the app was asking from the wrong point.
Candidate: I confirmed the fix by breaking the stream on purpose at different points, then reconnecting and checking that each day appeared once.
Candidate: I also ran it on a weak network and after killing the app, so the saved position was tested from a cold start.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: First, I could let the server keep the resume point, so the app sends nothing and the server decides where to continue.
Candidate: Second, I could ask for the whole plan again on every reconnect and replace everything on screen.
Candidate: I didn't pick the server-side point because the backend team was small and it added state to every request.
Candidate: I didn't pick the full reload because users would lose the cards they already had and wait again.
Candidate: I kept the client-side point, but saved it only after the card was drawn, and added the guard for a bad saved point.
Candidate: After release, I checked it with our tests and the logs from real users; they only cover the cases we saw, so they can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.
Candidate: The staged rollout also gives us a way to compare resume rates against fallback rates before everyone is exposed.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At KKday, on the AI trip planner, we had a delivery risk about two weeks before a release.
Candidate: The app team and I disagreed about what to do when a plan failed our checks.
Candidate: Retrying could give a complete plan, but users would wait longer.
Candidate: Showing an error at once was faster, but we might give up too early.
Candidate: I brought real failed examples and retry times to the people involved: the app team, the backend owner and product.
Candidate: I gave two options.
Candidate: First, retry up to a fixed limit, then show a safe fallback.
Candidate: Second, show the error immediately and let the user ask again.
Candidate: The product manager decided.
Candidate: I finished the retry limit and the fallback on the backend myself.
Candidate: The app team built the screen that shows the fallback.

Interviewer: On the KKday planner, you said product chose "retry up to a fixed limit, then show a safe fallback" — what risk were you willing to accept before that release, and who watched the data afterward? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: The risk I accepted was that some users would wait longer before they saw a plan.
Candidate: We kept the retry limit small, so the wait stayed short.
Candidate: The product manager and I watched the data after release.
Candidate: We looked at how often plans fell back and how often users asked again.
Candidate: If fallbacks had jumped, I'd have paused the rollout and rolled back.
Candidate: We also had a staged rollout, so we could compare before everyone was exposed.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design, a few questions.
Candidate: Is the balance held by us, or does money move on a bank or card rail?
Candidate: Which currencies do we support?
Candidate: What should work offline?
Candidate: And is our server ledger the single source of truth?
Candidate: Does that match what you want first?

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Here's the flow.
Candidate: The screen only shows state and sends user actions.
Candidate: The ViewModel holds the transfer state and calls the repository.
Candidate: The repository is the only place that talks to the server and the local database.
Candidate: The local database keeps the cached balance, the history and the transfer intent with its client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server's ledger is the only source of truth for balances; the app only shows what the server confirms.
[board] flowchart TD |   S[Screen] --> VM[ViewModel] |   VM --> R[Repository] |   R --> DB[Local DB] |   R --> API[Server API] |   API --> L[Server ledger]
Candidate: The transfer intent is saved in the local database before the request goes out.
Candidate: That way a lost response is an unknown outcome, not a failure.
Candidate: After a restart, the app asks the server by account and the same client transfer ID, and the server answers with the original transfer's status.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: I'll draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars.
Candidate: A confirms on a native screen first, and the app saves the intent with its client transfer ID before anything goes out.
Candidate: The server then debits A and credits B in one transaction, so A goes from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80.
Candidate: The result screen shows success only from the server's transfer record.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as A (app) |   participant S as Server |   participant L as Ledger |   A->>A: Confirm 80 dollars |   A->>A: Save intent + client ID |   A->>S: Transfer 8000 cents, client ID |   S->>L: Debit A, credit B (one transaction) |   L-->>S: Transfer record |   S-->>A: Status of that transfer |   A->>A: Show result from server record
Candidate: The amount goes over the wire as 8000 cents, a Long, not a float.
Candidate: And the result screen has four states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown while we're still checking.

Interviewer: You said the app saves the intent with its client transfer ID before the request goes out — what exactly gets written to the local database at that moment, and how does the app know later that this intent is still pending rather than done?
Candidate: I write one row for the transfer intent.
Candidate: It holds the client transfer ID, the payer and payee, the amount as 8000 cents, and a status of pending.
Candidate: The status only changes when the server's transfer record comes back.
Candidate: So after a restart, any row still marked pending is the one I look up by account and client ID.
Candidate: A lookup that finds nothing doesn't prove no money moved, so it stays unknown.
Candidate: The row also needs a timestamp and a retry count, so a stuck pending row can be found later.
Candidate: The status only moves to done when the server's transfer record comes back.

Interviewer: Your sequence has "S-->>A: Status of that transfer" and "Show result from server record," which both assume the response arrives. With the transfer committed but the response lost and the process killed, what changes when A reopens the app? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: The transfer is already committed, so the money has moved.
Candidate: The app just never heard back.
Candidate: When A reopens the app, the pending row is still there with its client ID.
Candidate: So the app asks the server for that same ID, and the server answers with the original transfer's status.
Candidate: Then the result screen shows success from the server's record, not from the lost response.
Candidate: I'd resend that same client ID only while the server's idempotency window still covers it; after that, I'd rely on the lookup and reconciliation, never a new ID.
